THE RESPONSES

• Reached by phone on Wednesday and asked about the relationship, Huang said, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly." He then hung up

NO DENIAL

THE COVER-UP IS THE FACT THAT MATTERS

Per three people briefed on the incident, Huang's security witnessed the bystander with their phone and sequestered them, and made the person an offer to sign a nondisclosure agreement. A relationship is a conduct problem. A security detail detaining a witness and buying silence is a concealment problem, and concealment is what boards and prosecutors actually act on.

posts.text:
Ian Buck (VP Hyperscale and high-performance computing) is the most likely Internal candidate.  

From Grok:  Buck is best known as the inventor of CUDA, $NVDA’s foundational software platform for general-purpose GPU computing.

He joined NVIDIA in 2004 after earning his PhD in computer science from Stanford University (thesis on stream computing on graphics hardware; advisor Pat Hanrahan). At Stanford he led development of Brook, a stream programming language that was a key precursor to general-purpose computing on GPUs (GPGPU). He also holds a BSE in computer science from Princeton University (summa cum laude, class of 1999).
In his current role, Buck leads the multi-billion-dollar datacenter business unit focused on AI and HPC products. He oversees AI hardware and software used by major hyperscalers and AI companies (including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, OpenAI, and others), manages product development, partnerships, and go-to-market strategy, and is a direct report to CEO Jensen Huang. He has described the evolution from individual chips to full “AI factory” / rack-scale systems as a core focus.

Why he matters: CUDA turned GPUs into programmable accelerators for scientific computing and, later, deep learning and generative AI. It became the standard platform used by millions of developers and is widely viewed as a key element of NVIDIA’s competitive advantage (often called its “moat”) in AI computing. Buck has testified before the U.S. Congress on AI, advised the White House, and works on national AI supercomputers. He is frequently cited in industry discussions of NVIDIA’s leadership and has appeared in reporting on potential internal succession candidates.

He regularly speaks at events such as GTC, OCP, and HPC conferences on topics including GPU data centers, agentic AI, power efficiency, and full-stack AI infrastructure.

Look at this.

Skeena Resources, $SKE, normally trades about 130 call options a day. Then, over three days in October, someone put more than $5 million into its December 2027 calls. They bought in chunks of 100 to 400 contracts, small enough to slip past flow alerts that only flag trades of 500 or more.

Open interest showed the buyer was holding on. It jumped from 827 to about 4,900 in the $32.50 calls and stayed there. A week later, the same pattern hit the $30 calls, and open interest there went from 69 to 2,186.

$NVDA (-4.4% AH):  Jensen Huang Said to Have Had Relationship With Nvidia Executive Who Reports to Him

Mr. Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, is already facing scrutiny over an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy.

New York Times
Ryan MacTripp Mickle and Georgia Gee
Nov. 11, 2026, 4:55 p.m. ET

Jensen Huang, the leader of Nvidia who is under investigation for an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy, also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reports to him, according to five people who worked at the company.

The relationship, which has not been previously reported, was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, said the people, who spoke under the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive information. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Many corporations have policies against managers having relationships with subordinates.

Mr. Huang, 63, and Ms. Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel during a Nvidia conference in March, according to two of the people who worked at the company. The New York Times has not seen the video.

Both Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell are married to other people.

Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has turned it into the premier supplier of artificial intelligence chips, has been under intensifying scrutiny. Last month, The New York Times reported that a Chinese executive he had become close to had been identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese intelligence asset.

This month, after Mr. Huang acknowledged the affair, Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into the matter that is being led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. The Republican leaders of three influential House committees have also asked Mr. Huang to appear for a closed-door briefingon his interactions with the woman, who goes by the name Alice Huang.

China has denied the espionage claims. Ms. Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.

When reached by phone Wednesday and asked about his relationship with Ms. Powell, Mr. Huang said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly.” He then hung up.

Nvidia declined to provide a statement. Ms. Powell did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE THE LEASH: WHY TRUMP PROTECTED JENSEN HUANG

Every account of the Jensen Huang affair asks the same question: how did the President of the United States embrace a man his own intelligence services believed was compromised by a Chinese spy? There is a simpler question underneath it. What if the knowledge was the point? What follows is the timeline, and the explanation it points to. Trump knew, early and in detail, and he held what he knew as leverage over the world’s most powerful man in artificial intelligence and business. The protection was never generosity. It was the price of the leash.

THE SETUP

• Alice Huang, a Chinese national, ran Megaspeed International, a Singapore company that customs data later showed moved at least $4.6 billion worth of restricted Nvidia chips toward China between 2023 and late 2025.
• Her relationship with Jensen Huang reportedly began in the spring of 2024 and deepened across two years of travel, dinners, and photographs.
• Singapore detained her in 2025, according to later reporting, and United States authorities were investigating her company while the relationship continued.

HE WAS TOLD TWICE

• November 2025: Trump is briefed on the relationship and on the intelligence assessment behind it. He takes no action.
• May 2026, on the way to the Beijing summit of May 13 to 15: Secretary of State Marco Rubio learns that Huang will join the presidential trip in Alaska and, before the pickup, briefs the President on the issue again. A United States government official has confirmed the briefing. It is the second warning in seven months.
• Huang boards in Alaska anyway and steps off in Beijing a few paces behind Rubio. The warning did not change the seating chart. It was never going to.

THE DISPLAYS

• August 2026: Trump reportedly calls into an internal Nvidia employee meeting, and Huang takes the call.
• September 14, 2026: on stage at the All-In Summit in Los Angeles, in front of thousands of people, a phone is brought to Huang in the middle of his interview. It is the President. Huang fumbles with the speakerphone, puts him on, and agrees along while Trump performs for the room.
• Read those calls plainly. A president does not interrupt the most valuable chief executive on earth, inside his own company and on a public stage, unless the interruption itself is the message. I ring, he answers. Everyone in both rooms understood the demonstration.

THE CHANNEL STAYED OPEN

• While the warnings sat in the file, Megaspeed kept shipping, and the machinery that could have stopped it was held still.
• The Treasury Department and the Pentagon pushed to place Megaspeed on the Entity List, the restriction list that would have shut the channel down. The Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, delayed the additions for two months, and the company has still never been listed.
• Confronted at a National Security Council meeting by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who asked how come Megaspeed was not on the entities list, Lutnick answered: I don't know. I will look into it. That is the whole enforcement record, in the secretary's own words.
• The Justice Department asked Commerce to pause and took the matter criminally, and that explanation deserves its weight. But an investigation that never lands, beside a listing that never happens, beside a channel that never closes, is not enforcement. It is a held sword.
• January 2026, after the first briefing: the clearance for the advanced chip sales to China that Huang had lobbied for takes effect, with the government taking a cut of the revenue. The favors flowed toward Huang the whole time he was exposed. That is what protection looks like when it is paid for in obedience rather than cash.

WHY HOLD IT

• A secret like this is an asset only while it is secret, and Trump did not own this one. The intelligence community did, and they were never his allies in it. They were Huang's pursuers and his own internal opposition.

posts.text:
$AAPL at $355 call wall

At/Below $355: $355 represents a massive Call Wall (high concentrated Call Open Interest / Gamma). Market makers who sold those $355 calls are long gamma near/below the strike, shorting into strength to keep the price pinned.   

Above $355 (The Gamma Flip Trigger): If AAPL secures a strong 3-minute / 15-minute candle close above $355, market maker hedging dynamics invert. Calls move deeper in-the-money, forcing dealers to rapidly buy underlying shares to cover expanding delta (accelerating a gamma squeeze).

posts.text:
$NBIS reports tomorrow before the open. $CRWV print last night suggested demand isn't the problem for neoclouds. 

For Nebius, the question is execution: can it ramp fast enough to hit a very aggressive year-end target?

What I need to see:

1. The ARR ramp ARR was $3B in June, and the year-end guide is $7–9B. Q3 exit ARR needs to land around $4.5B+ to keep that credible. If they cut this, nothing else matters.

2. Revenue and guide Consensus is ~$905M for Q3. The FY guide of $3.0–3.4B implies $1.1–1.5B in Q4. Hold it or raise it.

3. Connected power The guide is 800 MW–1 GW by year-end. I want Q3 connected power around 675 MW or higher, and no slippage at new sites.

4. Microsoft Bloomberg reported last week that Microsoft is tightening oversight of Nebius projects. I want management to address it directly and confirm the New Jersey deployment is on schedule.

5. Funding mix In Q2 they had $8B of cash and $9B+ of customer prepayments covering 50–60% of capex, but also raised ~$2.8B by selling stock (ATM). Against a $20–25B capex year, I want prepayment coverage holding, more asset-backed debt and less dilution.

Nebius is far less levered than CoreWeave. What it has to prove now is on-time delivery, because that's exactly where the Microsoft headlines hit.

Tech is starting to look seriously cheap.

Thursday was brutal:
• S&P 500: −4.4%
• Nasdaq Composite: −5.5%
• VIX: +69.7%, its third-largest daily jump since 1990.

Now look at the valuation reset.

As of November 3, the Nasdaq 100 was trading at around 19x forward earnings, its lowest valuation since October 2022 and roughly 22% below its five-year average.

And this happened while forward earnings estimates were rising. Citadel Securities reported Nasdaq 100 forward EPS estimates up 14% since June.

Prices falling while earnings expectations rise makes the valuation picture increasingly interesting. The key is whether those estimates hold.

Meanwhile, Morgan Stanley’s U.S. TMT momentum factor is approximately 62% below its 12-month high. That specific factor has suffered a deeper drawdown than during the dot-com bust.

The unwind in crowded tech trades has been extreme.

Then there’s the VIX.

Looking at the 10 previous occasions since 1990 when the VIX jumped at least 50% in one session:

• The S&P 500 was higher 21 trading days later in 9 out of 10 cases.
• The average return was +2.8%.
• Eight of those ten episodes still saw lower closing prices along the way.

Small sample, but an interesting signal. Further downside and an eventual rebound can both happen.

Friday already brought some relief:
• Nasdaq Composite: +1.1%
• Semiconductors: +4.2%
• VIX: −9.0% to 25.64.

A first bounce still needs follow-through.

My take: cheaper valuations, a severe momentum unwind and cool

$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE FOLLOW-UP TO THE CLEARING EVENT: AN INDUSTRY OUTGROWS ITS CHOKEPOINT

The Jensen Huang case stopped being an overhang this morning and became a clearing event. The GAI infrastructure complex is ripping, and the shape of the move is the story: the industry is being re-rated as bigger than the man. For months this complex carried a whisper discount: the case was known in fragments, in private hands, and a risk that cannot be discussed cannot be priced. Now it is public, on the record, and in the price, and the capital that opacity locked out can finally own the trade. What comes out the other side is a more durable industry than the one that went in.

THE TAPE, EARLY AFTERNOON

• CoreWeave up 26.4%. SanDisk up 16.8%. Lumentum up 14.8%. Dell up 14.5%. Micron up 13.6%.
• Credo up 13.0%. Coherent up 12.7%. Marvell up 12.6%. Super Micro up 11.9%. Vertiv up 8.9%.
• AMD up 8.8%. Arista up 7.1%. Broadcom up 7.0%. TSMC up 5.0%.
• Nvidia itself up 4.6%, lagging the semiconductor index at up 6.6%. The complex is not pricing a rescue of one company. It is pricing the removal of a discount from all of them.
• The complex faded mid-morning, took it all back by noon, and is pressing higher into the afternoon.

HOW ONE MAN BECAME THE CHOKEPOINT

• Allocation ran through one door. For two years the scarcest input in the world economy, leading edge AI compute, was allocated by one company, and the queue formed around one man's relationships, judgment and calendar. Sovereign funds, hyperscalers and startups all waited on the same Rolodex.
• The industry's political risk got personalized. Export controls, China exposure and Washington access for an entire sector came to be embodied in one person: his lobbying, his public advocacy, his travel. So when the questions turned personal, an investigation, a board probe, Senate letters, subpoena talk, the whole complex carried the discount for one man's legal and political exposure.
• He became the narrator of the buildout. Every capex guide, every earnings season, every supply headline was read through one man's commentary. His words moved the whole sector's multiple, up and down, because the market had outsourced its judgment of an industry to its most visible founder.
• And there was no visible second act inside the company. Founder and CEO since 1993, no designated successor, no president or chief operating officer, no other public face. The bench is deep, but it has never been introduced. An untested succession is an unpriced tail, and the market priced it every day without knowing it.

THE WHISPER DISCOUNT

• Part of the discount on this complex was never about fundamentals. It was an information discount. For months the case existed in fragments, in private hands: an investigation whispered about, a relationship photographed, a board quietly retaining counsel. A risk that lives in whispers cannot be priced properly, because the people who understand it best are the people least able to trade on it.
• That is the trap for tipped off money. Anyone who knew early held knowledge they could not build on. Trading size on an undisclosed investigation is exactly what the law prohibits, and no risk committee will approve a position whose thesis cannot be written down. So the informed stayed small or stayed out, the uninformed sold the rumor drip, and the discount fed on itself.
• Disclosure broke the trap. The letters are public. The board probe is public. The reporting is on the record. The risk is now what markets are built to handle: known, arguable, and incorporated into prices. And the capital that opacity locked out is finally permitted to own the trade.
• Look at who is buying, and how. Not a rescue bid for one company: the whole complex at once, led by the names furthest from the man, with his own stock up the least. That is institutional money underwriting a disclosed risk across a basket, the only way size can enter a story like this.

When I make a trade, my thinking is never about being right or even wrong. It's about risk vs. reward. I call it Bell Curve Thinking. I ask myself, if I make this trade 1000 times, does it come out a winner. Is it likely that the trade's upside is at least 2-3X the my stop?  If I get those right, the rest takes care of itself.
My most recent $SPY short is a perfect example. The stock fell 5X my stop. I had the opportunity to capture 5Rs. But that's precisely what afforded me to hold for a bigger move while improving my stop to breakeven. I made that decision based on the odds at the time.  If I turn out to be wrong... nothing lost. Next.

Nice to see $NBIS up +18% today (our biggest position) but this is just the beginning of the rally if they can post a strong earnings report tomorrow morning... stock needs to go up another +80% just to get back to where it was after Q2 earnings. 

From recent management commentary we know that $NBIS is likely done doing hyperscaler deals at ~$12M per MW because they used those deals to fund their capex and once they expire they'll be selling that capacity at $25-35M per MW on 2-3 year deals, $35-45M per MW on 1-2 year deals and $45M+ on short term deals. These are the current rates, they could go higher or lower over the next couple years. Important to remember that once those hyperscaler deals expire... the EBIT margins on the revenues from selling that capacity a second time could be ~80% or higher because they are paid for and fully depreciated (or close to it). 

$NBIS continues to raise their guidance for connected power which is currently at 5GW… with 800MW to 1GW of connected power by end of 2026 and plans to add at least 1GW of connected power every year which means they should be able to exit 2027 at 2GW of connected power. If they can get to 2GW by end of next year and the blended rate across all customers (hyperscalers and non-hyperscalers) is $20M per MW then $NBIS could exit 2027 at $40B ARR (or close to it) depending on timing of specific buildouts, permit approvals, hardware deliveries, potential bottlenecks, etc. If they get to 2GW of connected power and the blended rate across all customers is $25M (very possible) then $NBIS could exit 2027 at $50B ARR (also depends on timing of several factors).

There were lots of positive announcements in Q3, not going to cover all of them here but I suspect we get some updates tomorrow on the earnings call. I'm most interested in their asset light business/strategy and whether they've signed up any partners and what the economics of those deals might look like. There's still alot of bare-metal PSPs/HPCs with land & power but no software stack which is why they're doing colo deals with hyperscalers and frontier labs at $2-3M per MW.. however over the next couple years we could see them start to partner with $NBIS, license their stack and now those PSPs/HPCs are charging $20-30M per MW with $NBIS getting a 15% cut (I'm just guessing on this number).

$CRWV CEO said that demand is currently 10x higher than capacity... I suspect we hear something similar from $NBIS tomorrow. I also think it's possible we near about short term deals getting done above $50M per MW. 

Tomorrow should be fun... I'm betting our $NBIS investment thesis gets even stronger over the next 24 hours. 

Good luck to the $NBIS bulls...and to the $NBIS bears... get wrecked!!!

$SPCX If Anthropic leaves, SpaceX gets scarce compute back, and that's the part the bears are missing.

On the Q3 call, Musk said short-term compute contracts are renewing at higher dollars per watt and SpaceX could rent its compute "several times over" if it said yes to everyone. The CFO added that new deals are pricing slightly above the high end of the $30 to $50 per watt range.

Demand is there. Google already pays SpaceX about $920M a month, hyperscalers and dozens of smaller firms are asking for capacity, and Grok and Cursor can absorb whatever comes back. Musk's stated goal is roughly a 50/50 split between internal use and renting to others.

Pricing is also moving SpaceX's way. GPU rental rates rose about 7% in November, and Anthropic's own S-1 says its short-term compute costs significantly more than its multi-year deals.

The 90-day exit cuts both ways. Anthropic can walk once the non-cancelable periods end in January and March 2027, but so can SpaceX, and SpaceX is the one holding the scarce asset.

• Senator Richard Blumenthal plans a Senate investigation into Huang's relationship with the administration and its AI chip policy once Democrats take control of the chamber in January. He would chair the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, which carries broad subpoena power.
• Senator Chris Coons wants a probe into whether national security was compromised. Senator Mark Warner wants a full accounting of what the administration knew and when it knew it. Senator Jim Banks is drafting a bill to ban advanced AI chip exports to China outright.

$TSM $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE TAIWAN OCTOBER SALES: RECORDS ACROSS THE CHAIN

All 34 tracked companies have now reported October revenue. Aggregate NT$3,739.2B, up 6.9% month on month after a mixed September. Every company grew year on year and the median gain was about 47%. The month set records up and down the chain: an all-time high at TSMC, an all-time high at Foxconn, a twelfth straight monthly record at Nanya, a fourth straight record at Global Unichip. The AI hardware chain did not just grow into the fourth quarter. It accelerated.

THE MACRO CHECK

Taiwan's own trade data says the same thing. October exports hit a record $96.76 billion, up 58.9% year on year, the first month ever above $90 billion and the thirty-sixth straight month of year-on-year growth. Integrated circuit exports were NT$1.02 trillion. Imports also set a record, and semiconductor equipment imports rose 83.4% year on year to $4.92 billion: capacity is still being built, not harvested. The Ministry of Finance expects demand to stay strong through the fourth quarter, with geopolitics and US trade policy named as the risks.

FOUNDRY

TSMC printed the biggest month in its history: NT$586,890M, up 59.7% year on year and 14.7% month on month, about $17.9 billion. It topped August's previous record by NT$72 billion, was the first month above NT$550 billion and the third straight above NT$500 billion. Revenue for the first ten months, NT$4,485.6B, already exceeds the whole of 2025. TSMC gave no breakdown, but the guide math is informative: fourth-quarter guidance of $52.3 to $54.3 billion needs November and December to average roughly NT$538 to $570 billion, below October's pace. The guide embeds a sequential step-down from the October run rate, which leaves room to beat it. Management's recent framing is that output may fall short of demand in coming quarters. The constraint is supply, not orders.

Behind TSMC, the mature-node names confirm the shape: UMC up 18.3% year on year and flat on the month, steady rather than accelerating. Powerchip rose 94.2% year on year on the DRAM rebound. Vanguard VIS fell 20.2% on the month after rising 15.9% in September, 8-inch lumpiness with the trend intact at +20.5% year on year. This is a leading-edge cycle.

MEMORY

Nanya rose 487.7% year on year to a twelfth consecutive monthly record, and Winbond rose 257.0%. The detail that matters: this supercycle is price, not volume. Nanya's third-quarter selling prices rose about 60% in a single quarter while bit shipments fell by a mid-single-digit percentage, producing a gross margin of 85.7%. In October its shipments dipped again after it exhausted available inventory, while prices kept rising. Management expects prices to rise further in the fourth quarter, and AI infrastructure is now more than 20% of its revenue. The one caution in the memory tape is the same as last month: Nanya and Winbond grew only 3 to 4% month on month. Levels are still rising, but the rate of change has likely peaked.

AI SERVERS

The five big server makers reported NT$2.02 trillion of October revenue between them, up 60.9% year on year; excluding Foxconn, they nearly doubled, up 98.9%.

Foxconn's NT$1,305,320M was its highest month ever, up 45.7% year on year, and its ten-month total of NT$8.98 trillion is up 40.4%. Musings of the Day, 11/11/26:

Many are pointing to $CRWV’s prepaid deals as proof the DEBT GOVERNOR doesn’t bind AI compute. I’d respectfully submit the opposite.

1. Management’s own words: “We will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields.” That IS the Debt Governor talking. Cash interest hit $846M for the quarter, up from $310M a year ago, which is how a 62% Adj. EBITDA margin still became a $709M net loss.

2. The prepays are carrying the cash flow statement. Operating cash flow was $1.98B, while deferred revenue rose $2.13B. Strip out customers paying upfront and operations burned cash. A prepay is a LOAN from the customer, repaid in compute.

3. So who’s lending? OpenAI (funded by equity and increasingly debt) and the Hyperscalers, who’ve gone from funding ~9% of capex with new debt in 2024 to ~32% today. The Debt Governor didn’t disappear. It moved to the balance sheets writing the checks.

4. Customers only prepay when capacity is SCARCE. Hyperscalers with cheap IG capital and paid-off fleets use neoclouds as overflow in a boom and keep their own data centers full in a bust. If end demand merely grows slower than expected, the prepays vanish first, and the Bullwhip snaps hardest on the leveraged supplier furthest UPSTREAM -- like $CRWV.

The Tell: watch the share of deals that still come with prepays. When that fades while Hyperscaler borrowing keeps climbing, Credit is your Canary in the Coalmine.

posts.text:
$CRWV 新兴云服务商最新财报后暴涨，只是超跌反弹。

其实从上个季度财报 $NBIS 我第一时间就解读清楚什么是“新云”，核心投资逻辑，什么样的投资策略和估值仓位

市场情绪在中选后极度踩踏崩盘后，如何解读并预测？

政策这只手只能制造周期波动，不然搞政策最牛的中国为何经济拐点向下。核心还是看需求

你可以理解这种行业就是“算力专卖店”，直接卖的就是高密度GPU集群/电力/网络/快速交付/项目融资的系统化短平快AI算力交付

直接体现市场对于算力的供需冷暖“鸭先知”。现在市场对于算力需求爆棚，谁能先上线当然短期合同租金高涨，快速回本。和酒店在旺季提价一个道理

现在最新财报再一次证明算力需求的紧缺时期，从不断上涨的租金，7层需求都是已经有客户提前预付款，财富500强10%采购渗透。

这个至少短期极高的算力需求对于上游芯片存储互联都是利好和证据。而且也缓解市场普遍认为公司融资风险，还有就是老的GPU价值还在涨价

当然建设风险就是“融资提款在前、通电收费在后”的时间错配风险，是市场主要担心民主党所在。我也周报分析了，AI经济发展需要规范而不可能扼杀。这个是对选票负责，无论什么党。而且需求在，新建供给压缩，反而利好现有的租金

其他比如软件服务方面都是锦上添花。核心看着这种股票投资价值所在

典型的概念和期权性质股票，风险承受力高的可以考虑，分析这个股票价值，在于验证AI泡沫的程度。

具体颗粒度更细的对于新云公司的行业解读和投资策略估值区间见订阅者时间线搜索

当然如果只出租GPU，归根到底就是高杠杆、强周期、硬件快速折旧的数据中心运营商，不同在于AI爆发性的算力需求。

它们用客户合同和预付款证券化未来算力需求，用融资购买电力、GPU 和时间，再通过集群软件把硬件转化成有效 Token。

短期利润来自稀缺高租金，长期价值则取决于能否从 GPU 小时收费升级为 Token、软件和工作流收费。

如果升级失败，它们最终只是高杠杆、强周期的数据中心运营商。如果升级成功，它们将成为介于英伟达、云大厂和 AI 应用之间的新型第三方算力提供商模式

当然它的成功就是英伟达的成功，避免被人家说什么循环融资，英伟达也不希望任何单一云厂商控制 AI 算力入口，特别是云大厂现在也搞自研的芯片。

$RKLB Rocket Lab's laser terminals are now derisked.

Mynaric's CONDOR Mk3 terminal just completed a bidirectional optical link from space to the ground, sending files both up to orbit and down to Earth. It flew on SES's meoSphere Pathfinder 1 mission aboard a K2 Space Mega-class satellite and connected to a Cailabs ground station.

Optical terminals are a key part of its SDA constellation satellites, and Mynaric is the in-house supplier it bought to vertically integrate them. 

After years of CONDOR delays, a flight-proven link with SES as a customer outside Rocket Lab is a massive step.

posts.name: BlindSquirrelMacro
posts.text: Fun story. In about 2010/2011, Soros (yes, that one) did a bunch of work and back-testing and came to the conclusion that they would participate in every ECM transaction on the street (globally). They came to all the big IBs and said that they would take 1% of every transaction we led. After 18 months, they realised that they were getting 1% of 100% of all the 'dogs' and 0.75% (or less) of all of the good deals. There was always an excuse from the syndicate desks as to why they could not get their 'quota' on the hot ones - "management were heavily involved in allocation"; "management really hacked back the hedge funds. sorry" were the usual excuse. That allocation delta was enough to make the strategy a loss-maker. They quietly dropped the idea after about 18 months. Now just imagine employing a similar strategy as a retail investor.... @BenBrey $ANT #foiegrasgeese

posts.text:
Will seasonality and cyclical tendencies bail the market out as we head into two of the stronger months of the year?

UPDATE: On October 15, I added the $SPY short to our portfolio in anticipation of a general market decline. At the time, the position was initiated as a hedge against our long exposure.
Since then, the market declined, with the $QQQ falling 11% and the $SPY declining 5% from our entry price (short). That weakness stopped us out of all but one of our long positions ($TEVA) - either at small losses or with profits on stocks where we had backstopped gains.
By default, as our long exposure came down, the $SPY short transitioned from being a hedge to leaving us net short the market.
We view the recent action as a stealth bear market in certain areas, where the major indexes have masked significant deterioration beneath the surface, particularly among AI infrastructure and technology stocks. Many of those names have suffered substantial declines from their highs, driving them to oversold levels.
My original stop on the $SPY was 778.00, which represented a new all-time high only about 1% above our short price. I have now improved that stop to our breakeven price of 769.64, eliminating stop-loss risk on the position.
The trade has already been a success from a risk/reward standpoint. We initially risked approximately 1%, while the $SPY declined roughly 5% from our entry—about a 5R move. 
Our decision to hold for a potentially larger move was based first on the position serving as a hedge and, subsequently, on our ability to de-risk the trade to the point where we now have zero principal risk.
This is a classic way I approach many of my market/ETF trades when shorting the general market.

$AKAM KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM AKAMAI TECHNOLOGIES’ Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Akamai’s November 5 call supports a selective investment conclusion: AI infrastructure spending is broadening beyond GPUs, but the associated economic benefits accrue to different companies at different stages. Component suppliers and manufacturing partners can receive orders and cash well before cloud operators recognize revenue or earn acceptable returns on invested capital. The approximately $30 million deployment-related revenue deferral does not establish weaker underlying demand; the planned $1.7 billion component purchase illustrates that procurement can accelerate while customer billing slips. The highest-conviction implications concern customer-funded manufacturing, server memory, established CPU suppliers, PC input-cost pressure, CDN pricing discipline, application security, and available colocation capacity. Several relationships were disclosed before this earnings call, making November’s contribution confirmation of execution rather than an entirely new order announcement.

ELECTRONICS MANUFACTURING AND SERVER SYSTEMS

CUSTOMER-FUNDED COMPONENT INVENTORY IMPROVES JABIL’S EXPOSURE TO THE AI BUILDOUT (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: Jabil Inc. (JBL: US). Direction: positive. Magnitude: meaningful program-level opportunity and favorable working-capital protection; the incremental consolidated earnings contribution remains undisclosed.

Call evidence: Akamai reiterated that it expects to spend approximately $1.7 billion in Q4 2026 to “secure and pre-purchase critical supply chain components, notably memory.” Management also stated that approximately 70% of the hardware, memory, and other components required for the latest Anthropic agreement had been secured.

The decisive supplier connection appears in Akamai’s September contractual disclosure. Jabil was authorized to purchase approximately $1.7 billion of memory components, with Akamai paying the corresponding supplier invoices when Jabil receives the components. Pending use, Jabil holds the inventory on consignment for Akamai and repurchases it at cost as it is consumed in production.

The transmission mechanism is therefore more attractive than a generic increase in contract-manufacturing orders. Akamai funds the advance component stockpile, reducing Jabil’s exposure to carrying that inventory during the interval before server assembly. Jabil retains manufacturing, integration, warranty, spare-parts, and repair opportunities without necessarily financing the entire early procurement requirement. This structure transfers an important portion of the inventory-financing burden toward the infrastructure owner.

The $1.7 billion authorization is equivalent to approximately 4.7% of Jabil’s roughly $36 billion fiscal 2026 revenue, demonstrating the program’s scale. It is not evidence of $1.7 billion of immediate incremental Jabil revenue, nor should Jabil’s corporate operating margin be applied to that amount. Component pass-through, consignment accounting, manufacturing fees, and shipment acceptance determine the actual revenue and profit contribution.

Near-term catalyst: component receipts, funding, and subsequent manufacturing conversion during Q4 2026 and early 2027. The agreement preceded Jabil’s September 30 fiscal 2027 outlook, so adding the entire procurement amount to existing guidance would risk double counting. Longer-duration implication: customer-funded procurement can make selected manufacturing exposures economically preferable to owning the infrastructure itself, particularly when cloud billing and returns are back-end-weighted.

$NRG KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM NRG ENERGY’S Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

NRG’s November 9 call reinforces a differentiated power-market outlook rather than a uniformly bullish AI-electricity thesis. Near-term ERCOT supply remains abundant, while PJM offers stronger medium-term earnings opportunities as legacy hedges expire. Simultaneously, the economics of serving large data centers are shifting toward customer-backed generation, substantial fixed capacity payments, and partnerships that share construction funding. The strongest positive implications are for scarce turbine capacity, operating dispatchable assets, and established developers capable of delivering financeable projects. The principal negatives concern premature expectations for Texas merchant-price recovery and valuations that treat undeveloped power capacity as equivalent to operating infrastructure. Peer disclosures available through November 10 indicate that several themes already underpin company guidance; NRG’s commentary often provides corroboration rather than a new earnings catalyst.

INDEPENDENT POWER PRODUCERS

ERCOT WEAKNESS CHALLENGES THE RECOVERY TRADE MORE THAN NEAR-TERM EARNINGS (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected company: Vistra Corp. (VST: United States). Directional impact: Negative for unhedged Texas generation margins and aggressive recovery assumptions; limited immediate impact on substantially hedged 2027 earnings. Magnitude: Moderate for medium-term valuation, potentially material for exposed generation margins, but insufficient evidence for a consolidated earnings downgrade.

Supporting commentary: NRG reported that year-to-date ERCOT prices averaged nearly 40% below its original planning assumption. Management explained that “battery build and solar have kind of dominated” recent additions and that demand “hasn’t been fast enough to absorb all of it.” NRG’s 2027 outlook includes $185 million of net wholesale-price pressure, primarily from ERCOT, partially offset by PJM.

Transmission mechanism: Additional solar depresses daytime energy prices, while batteries reduce the duration and frequency of high-price periods. Thermal generators can therefore experience weak realized margins even when annual electricity demand and peak demand are growing. For Vistra, the relevant exposure is the residual unhedged Texas generation margin after fuel, retail obligations, and financial hedges, not gross ERCOT capacity.

The critical offset is Vistra’s own November 6 disclosure that approximately 98% of expected 2027 generation and 78% of expected 2028 generation were hedged. These are company-wide percentages, not Texas-specific measures, but they demonstrate why NRG’s weak-market commentary should not be translated directly into a large 2027 Vistra earnings reduction. Vistra also raised its 2026 EBITDA midpoint before NRG’s call. Existing hedges, capacity revenues, acquired assets, and the retail business can support earnings despite weak Texas spot markets.

Near-term trading implication: The call is negative for expectations of an imminent ERCOT-driven earnings upgrade, not a strong basis for forecasting an immediate Vistra earnings miss. The more consequential catalysts are changes in 2028 forward spark spreads and subsequent disclosures of regional hedge coverage.

Longer-duration implication: Demand must absorb renewable and storage additions before merchant generators receive the full benefit of Texas load growth. Population growth and large interconnection queues are not substitutes for evidence of improving hourly residual demand and retained generation margins.

$SANM KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM SANMINA’S Q4 FISCAL 2026 EARNINGS CALL

Sanmina’s November 9 call strengthens the case that AI infrastructure demand is progressing from engineering and qualification into a broader production cycle encompassing accelerators, networking, cooling, electrical distribution, and advanced manufacturing. The most consequential positive signal is commercial progress on AMD’s Helios platform, supported by initial shipments and customer wins across multiple customer categories. The most important negative signal is that accelerating demand requires substantial capital before producing distributable cash. Sanmina’s unusually strong quarterly margin also contains benefits that should not be extrapolated across its peers. The highest-conviction implications therefore favor verified component and infrastructure exposure while distinguishing production growth from cash conversion and customer returns. Most affected companies had already reported strong demand before this call, making Sanmina’s disclosures corroborating evidence rather than automatically new earnings upgrades. Country labels below indicate corporate domicile.

AI ACCELERATORS AND SYSTEMS NETWORKING

AMD’S RACK-SCALE COMMERCIALIZATION RISK IS DECLINING, BUT THE VOLUME RAMP REMAINS A 2027 EVENT (READ-THROUGH 1)

Advanced Micro Devices (AMD: United States). Direction: positive. Magnitude: high strategic significance and moderate incremental support for 2027 Data Center earnings expectations, with limited evidence for an additional near-term estimate increase.

The decisive commentary was Jon Faust’s statement that Sanmina had “now begun to ship the Helios product, albeit in small quantities.” Management also reported wins with hyperscalers, frontier AI laboratories, and OEMs, finalized operating models for several customers, and preliminary production schedules. These disclosures reduce the risk that AMD’s rack-scale opportunity remains constrained to component availability, demonstrations, or unqualified designs.

The transmission mechanism is manufacturing execution. Commercial accelerator adoption requires more than competitive silicon: customers need integrated racks, qualified cooling, reliable interconnects, production testing, and acceptable deployment times. Sanmina’s completed investments in power, liquid cooling, test cells, and automation address these constraints. Successful rack production supports shipments of AMD accelerators and associated processors and networking silicon, while providing customers with a more credible alternative platform.

The magnitude must be assessed against the correct baseline. Sanmina expects cloud and AI systems revenue of $7.5 billion to $9.0 billion in fiscal 2027, versus approximately $5.3 billion in fiscal 2026. The midpoint implies approximately 56% growth. However, this category includes non-AMD platforms and other products, and its net consignment accounting prevents conversion into an AMD semiconductor revenue forecast.

AMD had already reported on November 3 that Data Center revenue reached $8.5 billion and that Helios production was scaling. Sanmina therefore independently corroborates commercialization rather than revealing an entirely new launch. Its second-half-weighted outlook also does not establish a contradiction with AMD’s nearer-term ramp: semiconductor shipments, rack assembly, and customer acceptance can occur in different periods.

Near-term catalysts are customer acceptance milestones and Sanmina’s next quarterly systems-revenue update. The longer-duration implication is a reduction in the manufacturing and deployment barriers protecting the incumbent accelerator ecosystem. This is a competitive negative for NVIDIA (NVDA: United States), but the call establishes neither lost NVIDIA orders nor a basis for cutting NVIDIA’s near-term revenue forecast.

Revenue growth of 39%, net retention of 122%, and consumption-driven upside support that conclusion. They do not establish that Cloudflare’s unnamed competitors lost particular contracts, that agent traffic automatically creates advertising revenue, or that efficient application execution reduces aggregate demand for AI hardware.

The assertion that “the zero-trust vendors effectively just become features within what is a much larger platform play” identifies the commercial threat: security can become an expansion product within a broader infrastructure relationship rather than a separately contested purchasing decision.

The transmission mechanism to Zscaler is reduced exclusivity over the enterprise security buying process. $CRWV KEY READ-THROUGHS FROM COREWEAVE’S Q3 2026 EARNINGS CALL

CoreWeave’s results reinforce a positive demand signal for AI infrastructure, but the more consequential market implication is widening differentiation between operating assets, financed construction, and unfunded development pipelines. Stronger GPU pricing, premium renewals, and substantial customer prepayments improve the economics of installed capacity and reduce near-term counterparty concerns for suppliers and landlords. However, management’s rejection of unsecured borrowing at current yields confirms that demand alone does not make expansion financeable. The strongest positive read-throughs concern contracted landlords, competing clouds with capacity available for repricing, NVIDIA’s infrastructure ecosystem, and enterprise storage. The clearest negative implications concern unfunded expansion and the assumption that incumbent x86 suppliers will automatically capture the CPU requirements of agentic AI. Magnitudes below refer to business and valuation exposure, not predicted share-price moves. Country labels identify primary listing markets.

AI CLOUDS, DATA-CENTER LANDLORDS AND FINANCING

CONTRACTED LANDLORDS RECEIVE CREDIT RELIEF, NOT AUTOMATIC RENT INCREASES (READ-THROUGH 1)

Affected companies: Core Scientific (CORZ: US); Applied Digital (APLD: US).

Direction and magnitude: Positive. High relevance to Core Scientific’s current earnings stream and meaningful relevance to Applied Digital’s operating portfolio. The immediate effect is primarily a reduction in perceived counterparty risk rather than an increase in contractual rental revenue.

CoreWeave expects approximately $9 billion of customer prepayments and deposits over the next 3 months, including more than $3 billion associated with existing, debt-repaid infrastructure. Management also stated that existing customer commitments should generate sufficient cash to service and repay both asset-level and parent-level debt before renewals. These disclosures strengthen the prospective cash resources available to meet facility obligations, although expected receipts are not equivalent to cash already collected.

The direct exposure is substantial. Core Scientific’s November 5 disclosures identified 590 MW contracted to CoreWeave, with 485 MW already billing and approximately 100 MW approaching delivery. Core Scientific stated that CoreWeave had funded the overwhelming majority of the construction expenditure. That upfront investment also reduced CoreWeave’s ongoing lease rate, making the facilities economically attractive to retain. Improved CoreWeave liquidity therefore supports an established, relatively low-occupancy-cost revenue stream rather than merely validating a speculative future tenant.

Applied Digital’s Polaris Forge 1 is leased to CoreWeave and comprises 400 MW across its completed and planned buildings. By October 1, 250 MW was operational. The campus represents approximately 28% of Applied Digital’s 1.41 GW of leased critical IT capacity, but a larger proportion of its currently operating AI-factory footprint. $NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE FIRST SENATOR CALLS FOR JENSEN HUANG TO RESIGN

THE NEWS

Senator Kevin Cramer of North Dakota, a senior Republican on the Senate Banking Committee, is calling for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to step down.

His reason is extortion risk. "The potential for extortion is so tremendous that something as sensitive as Nvidia chips, I just think he's got to go."

"If the worst thing he did in real life is infidelity with this woman who may or may not be a Chinese spy, but she might be, that's enough, because whatever else there is, we don't know. And to me, that's a security risk."

WHY IT IS DIFFERENT

Every congressional move until tonight was process: a closed-door briefing request for November 18, a subpoena threat if Huang does not answer by November 11, statements raising questions. This is the first demand for the man himself, and the first from a Republican, one day after the President publicly vouched for Huang.

Cramer sits on the committee with export control jurisdiction. This is not a backbencher freelancing.

THE ARGUMENT THAT MATTERS

The open question in this case has been knowledge: did Huang know of the intelligence concerns and intervene anyway. There is still no new evidence on that.

Cramer's case does not need it. It runs on compromise alone: a relationship with a possible foreign intelligence asset is itself the disqualifier, because of what could be held over the CEO of the company that makes the world's most sensitive chips.

That opens a second path to an exit, one already supported by the reported record, and it gives every other Republican cover. Joining a call costs far less than starting one.

THE LIMITS

One senator, speaking to a reporter. No letter, no hearing demand, no second name yet.

The relationship itself remains reported, not confirmed by any primary source. The decision channel is still the board's outside investigation, which has not reported.

THE READ

Probability of an announced resignation or removal: 30% by December 31, 2026, 45% by June 30, 2027, 50% by December 31, 2027. Up from 25/40/50.

What moves it further: a second senator joining, an institutional step by the Banking or Homeland Security committees, or any daylight between the White House and its vouching.

Huang's answer on the November 18 briefing is due tomorrow, November 11.

5 Critical Questions We Should Be Asking About The Jensen Huang Intelligence Revelations

1.  Who had the strongest incentive to leak this intelligence, and why now?

Was this an effort by U.S. intelligence officials to force action the administration was unwilling to take, a politically motivated attempt to undermine Trump and Huang, a Chinese operation to discredit a compromised relationship, or an effort by commercial interests to destabilize Nvidia? Who benefited most from the timing?

2.  If U.S. intelligence had identified a legitimate Chinese counterintelligence threat, why wasn’t Huang privately warned or approached for cooperation?

Why wasn’t a defensive briefing conducted, or the possibility of using the relationship for controlled intelligence collection explored? Was that option considered and rejected because of operational risks, or did someone deliberately prefer public exposure over quietly exploiting a potentially valuable intelligence opportunity?

3.  What did Trump, Rubio, the FBI, and other senior officials actually know, when did they know it, and who decided not to act?

If classified assessments had circulated months before the media revelations, what explains the apparent lack of intervention? Were national security concerns subordinated to Nvidia’s economic importance, U.S. semiconductor strategy, or Huang’s political relationships? And was there disagreement within the intelligence community over how to proceed?

4. Why was sensitive intelligence disclosed through anonymous media sources rather than established counterintelligence and congressional oversight channels?

If surveillance was ongoing, public exposure could compromise intelligence sources, alert foreign operatives, and destroy opportunities for further collection. Who determined that those risks were worth taking? Was the objective genuinely to protect national security, or to manufacture political and institutional pressure that could not otherwise be achieved?

5.  What major political, geopolitical, financial, or technological decisions were approaching when this information surfaced, and who stood to gain from the consequences?

Could the timing influence advanced semiconductor exports, negotiations with China, Nvidia’s leadership, congressional investigations, or broader U.S. AI policy? Were there unusual financial positions established before publication? Most importantly, was this simply the disclosure of a legitimate security concern, or was intelligence selectively exposed to influence a much larger strategic outcome?

The central issue is not whether any particular conspiracy theory is correct. It is whether the intelligence was handled primarily to protect national security or whether its disclosure served other interests. Until the underlying evidence, decision making timeline, and source of the leaks are established, those questions remain unanswered.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Sixty Years Above 2%, and Now the Fed Panics?

Services always run hot. Goods are doing their job. Oil is the shock.

Wall Street and the Fed are freaking out over services inflation, a number that has run above 2% for most of modern history. Since 1960, PCE services prices have topped 2% in 86% of months. Even in the 2010s, the decade we now remember as "too low" inflation, services ran above 2% three-quarters of the time. Today they sit at 3.5%, a flat 3.3 to 3.5% band for a year and well below the 6% peak of 2023.

The 2% target was never met because services behaved. It was met because goods deflated. From 1995 to 2019, core goods CPI ran at or below 2% in 96% of months and below zero 41% of the time. In the 2010s, the median was negative.

Look at the latest CPI. Core goods are running at just 0.7% year over year and rose only 0.2% in October. They've drifted down from 1.4% over the past year. Used cars are down 3.3% and new vehicles are up 0.7%. Tariff-sensitive items like furniture and appliances ticked up for the month, but furnishings are just 0.2% over the year. This is the old pattern returning: goods anchor, services carry.

The 4.6% jump in all-goods inflation is the oil shock. Energy goods are up 35%, and gasoline is up 37%. That's a negative supply shock, and the Fed's overnight rate can't drill a well, reopen a shipping lane or end a war.

Hiking into this mistakes supply for demand. Higher rates choke housing supply, which keeps shelter sticky, while Main Street and the cyclical economy outside AI pay the price.

The Fed is a sledgehammer, not a fine-tuning machine. Look past the oil shock, respect a century of services history, and let productivity do the work.

Some trivia or something most of you would never know abour me. 
In the 1980's, I manufactured and distributed one of the earlier widely commercialized blackjack strategy cards. It was on credit card plastic and meant to be handheld to help players with basic strategy. This was one of the earlier versions meant for single deck play. It was available in vending machines and gift shops in Atlantic City at the airport and on the boardwalk. 
At the time, I also wrote articles for a magazine called gambling times. In exchange, they traded me advertising space for the Blackjack Card.  I was just 22 years old.

Dan Schulman (CEO): “Satellite can’t compete in suburban or urban where 98% of our revenues are. And I made that point. They just can’t. We’re like a 100 to a thousand times more efficient and a better service.”

“If he builds a full terrestrial network just like we have, which is a very difficult proposition, or buys, whatever it may be, then you can compete. But that’s a very difficult proposition to go do. I’m prepared for it.”

“From a satellite perspective, it’s complementary. They’re extremely good in very rural areas or airplanes or boats. We don’t have a network there, and we never will build a network. We’re extremely good where most people are, in suburban and urban.”

“You could connect the two of those up and create a value prop where if you’re going to walk in a national forest and you have Verizon service, you’ll never be out of coverage. And I think that’s a really good value prop that we can work with the satellite companies on.”

JUST IN: Verizon CEO says SpaceX would need over $300 billion and four to six years to build a mobile network, which would make Elon Musk the sixth entrant in the market

Dan Schulman (CEO): “I think the right thing to do is to believe everything that SpaceX says they’re gonna do that they could do, and they do it with excellence. I think that there’s no downside to thinking that and preparing for that.”

“The downside is when you’re complacent about it, like, ‘ah, probably won’t happen, let’s not worry about it right now.’ You wanna be eyes wide open, ready.”

“As I mentioned yesterday, there’s the potential that he creates a mobile and broadband network. I think it will take four to six years for that to happen. I think it will cost $300 billion plus of capital.”

Google has unveiled TPU 8i Max, aka Whalefish. One interesting detail is that the announcement confirms the 8i Max will have 384GB of HBM per chip, meaning it moves to 8-hi HBM compared to the 12-hi HBM used for the original TPU 8i, which we reported to Accelerator Model subscribers several months ago. This follows Nvidia's move to move to 8-hi HBM for next generation Rubin Ultra.

Google is advertising much stronger inference performance TPU 8i Max as each package now has double the HBM bandwidth. Bandwidth is more important than capacity for inference performance as we explained recently in our 4-hi HBM article which you can read here: https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/long-live-the-short-king-why-4-hi

posts.name: John Arnold
posts.text:
Voters sent a clear message last week that they are deeply concerned about affordability. The rising costs of healthcare, housing & energy are putting real pressure on families.

But affordability can't just be a campaign slogan; it must be a governing philosophy. There are two main ways to address high costs: subsidies and supply side reforms. 

Subsidies have their place, but also serious problems, particularly in an environment of limited fiscal capacity with $2 tln annual deficits and the 10-year at 5%. More importantly, subsidies often treat the symptoms of high costs rather than their causes. 

Supply side reforms address the underlying problem. They expand capacity and competition, reduce costs for all Americans and do so without adding to the national debt.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is among the most important energy affordability bills this century. It helps the energy system deliver on multiple priorities by lowering costs, improving reliability, reducing emissions, creating jobs, strengthening energy independence, and supporting economic growth.

These goals transcend party lines. That's why two Democrats and two Republicans, representing very different states, ideologies and priorities, were able to negotiate a comprehensive bill that provides greater certainty for projects and streamlines environmental reviews while preserving the right to raise and adjudicate legitimate objections. It's also why the bill received 73 votes in the Senate yesterday, the first of several votes needed to make it law.

This bill is not perfect. No bill is. It includes some Republican priorities and some Democratic priorities. But mostly it includes American priorities that aren't partisan, like ensuring data centers pay 100% or more of their costs, establishing clear rules for responsible development, limiting executive authority to favor one energy source over another, and making better use of the infrastructure we've already built.

Politicians spent months telling voters they understood their concerns about affordability. Now they have a chance to prove it.

posts.name: Michael McDonough
posts.text:
Some fun: When has the market looked like this before?

I took the current cross-asset regime — equities, rates, credit, FX, commodities and volatility — and compared it with historical 63-trading-day periods based on both the direction and magnitude of market moves.

The closest historical match to November 2026?

April 2005 — 81% similarity.

What I found especially interesting is that it passes the macro smell test as well. Both periods combine relatively strong growth, elevated inflation, restrictive/tightening conditions, a fairly flat positive yield curve and credit markets that are not signaling acute stress.

That does not mean 2026 = 2005. There are some very important differences, particularly around housing and equity valuations.

So I also looked at what happened after the closest historical regimes.

Across the closest analogues, the median S&P 500 path was:

+2.0% after 1 month
+5.7% after 3 months
+3.4% after 6 months
+11.6% after 12 months
But the individual paths vary enormously — which is really the point.

Historical analogues aren't forecasts. They are a way of asking: when markets have been pricing a similar combination of growth, inflation, rates, credit and risk before, what happened next?

Still experimenting with this, but I think there is something pretty interesting here.

Saudi Arabia has been exporting crude so far this month at a rate that suggests the kingdom has lifted its oil production toward the 9-10 million b/d range.

Using both the Persian Gulf and (more importantly) the Red Sea, Riyadh has boosted crude exports during the first 22 days of October to >7 million b/d, reaching pre-war levels (see @Vortexa chart below). Adding clean and dirty refined product, the export flow Oct 1-22 reaches ~8.5m b/d, slightly below pre-war levels of >9m b/d. 

The crude export surge -- and the production boost -- could be part of a "use-while-you-can" strategy aimed at pumping ahead of the potential restart of the war post US midterms (or before the Houthis of Yemen damage another key oil installation -- several near misses already in recent days, including an attack that killed two contractors near a major oilfield).

Note: using Oct 1-2 as typically it takes at least five days for dark transits across the SoH to become clear.

posts.text:
메모리 제조사들은 TSMC의 가격 책정 방식을 보고 배우라는 얼토당토않은 얘기가 자꾸 나와서 글을 추가로 적어봄.

일단 DRAM은 수십 MB 이상의 메모리가 필요한 거의 모든 컴퓨팅 기기에 필수적으로 들어가는 부품임. 사실상 컴퓨터 산업의 원자재 같은 존재이고, 그래서 '산업의 쌀'이라고도 불림.

DRAM은 고객별 수요에 맞춰 생산하기보다는 표준화된 제품을 대량 생산하고, 고객들이 시장의 수급 상황에 따라 형성된 가격으로 구매하는 구조에 가까움. 즉 일반적인 제조업보다는 원자재 시장의 특성이 강함.

반면 파운드리는 철저히 고객의 요구에 맞춰 생산하는 산업임. 동일한 공정 노드라도 고객에 따라 사용하는 소재나 공정 구성이 달라질 수 있음.

따라서 팹을 구축하고 운영할 때부터 어떤 소재를 사용할지, 라인을 어떻게 구성할지, 설비를 어떻게 배분할지 등에 대한 구체적인 수요 예측이 중요함. 반대로 확실한 고객 수요를 확보할수록 불필요한 투자를 줄이고 고객 맞춤형으로 팹을 운영할 수 있다는 의미이기도 함.

가격 결정 구조도 다름.

파운드리는 특정 노드의 가격이 지나치게 올라가면 고객이 이전 세대 노드를 선택하거나 설계를 변경하는 등의 대안을 검토할 수 있음.

하지만 메모리는 다름. 메모리 없이 컴퓨팅 완제품을 생산하는 건 사실상 불가능하기 때문에, 가격이 아무리 올라가더라도 사업을 지속하려면 일정 물량은 반드시 확보해야 함.

메모리 제조사들이 의도적으로 가격을 낮게 책정한다고 해도 공급이 부족하면 물량 확보가 절실한 고객들은 결국 웃돈을 주고서라도 구매하려 할 것임. 이런 상황에서 제조사가 시장가격보다 싸게 팔 이유도 없음.

TSMC가 갑자기 2나노 공정 가격을 두 배로 올린다면 고객사들이 무조건 그 가격을 받아들일까? 반대로 모든 메모리 제조사가 가격을 두 배로 올린다면 고객사들이 구매를 거부하고 버틸 수 있을까?

물론 장기적으로는 메모리 역시 수요 감소나 대체 기술의 영향을 받겠지만, 단기적으로는 필수재라는 특성 때문에 가격에 대한 대응 방식이 근본적으로 다름.

간단히 비유하면 메모리는 석유이고 파운드리는 고품질 플라스틱에 가까움.

플라스틱이 더 높은 부가가치를 창출할 수는 있지만, 석유는 가격이 아무리 올라도 사용량을 줄일지언정 완전히 구매를 중단하기 어려움.

결국 두 산업은 수요 구조와 가격 결정 메커니즘 자체가 다른데, 단순히 TSMC처럼 가격을 책정하라는 건 산업의 본질적인 차이조차 모르는 무식한 발언임.

위 기사를 보고 반도체 생산 절대강자 TSMC도 납득가능한선에서 가격을 올리는데 메모리업체들은 뭘믿고 지금의 이익을 누리냐라는 의견들이 많다. 그런 의견들에 대한 반론이다.

당연히 지금같은 미친듯한 메모리 Shortage 발생시 파운드리가 메모리 이익을 따라잡을수가 없음

[본문]
1. 파운드리는 선발주 후생산 시스템이고, 메모리반도체는 선생산 후발주 시스템이다. 파운드리는 팹 증설부터 제조사와 고객사가 Risk를 나눠갖지만 메모리는 제조사가 Risk를 온전히 가져가는 시스템이다. 

2. 파운드리는 각 FAB이 초기 증설시 고객사의 요구가 많이 반영되기 때문에 시간이 지나 선단공정으로 전환하는게 메모리 대비 훨씬 어렵다. 그렇기때문에 메모리업체들이 Legacy 라인들을 최신라인으로 전환하며 이익률을 높일때 파운드리는 그러한 변화가 상대적으로 더 어렵다.

3. 또한, 위와같은 특성때문에 파운드리는 고객사와의 LTA가 기본적으로 맺어져 있어 가격을 무작정 올릴수는 없다. 다만, TSMC는 추가로 생산을 원하거나 납기를 단축시키고 싶은 고객을 위해 가격 프리미엄을 낼 수 있는 시스템을 운영하고 있다. 즉 고객이 돈만 충분하면 더 비싸게 주고 사갈수 있다는 뜻이고 그거까지 반영된게 현재의 영업이익이다.

4. 원래 '기술적 독점'기업은 가격을 조정할 수 있지만 후발주자의 추격때문에 가격의 상승은 보통 점진적으로 이뤄진다. 만약 메모리처럼 몇배수준으로 가격을 올린다면 당연히 고객사들은 삼성같은 후발주자로 눈을 돌리거나 선단공정 도입을 꺼리게 된다. 

5. 반면 메모리 3개 과점업체들은 모두 선생산 후발주 시스템으로 표준에 맞는 반도체를 미리 생산하고 시장에서 매겨진 가격으로 파는 형태이다. 특히 업체들간 기술적 차이는 파운드리만큼 크지 않고 매출과 영업이익은 보통 생산Capa에 비례한다. 구매자 또한 표준규격의 성능을 기대하고 메모리를 구입하므로 공급사간 차이를 크게 느끼지 못한다(요즘은 조금 달라지고 있긴 함). 

6. 이러한 메모리의 선생산 후발주 시스템으로 인해 시장의 공급은 생산Capa에 맞춰져 있고 수요만 변동되므로 원자재 가격처럼 움직인다. 당연히 수요가 미친듯이 올라가면 공급도 따라 올라가게된다. 

7. 다만, 문제는 FAB을 증설할때 비용이 굉장히 많이 들기때문에 기본적으로 10만~20만 Wafer 투입량 증량을 생각하고 투자하게 된다. 또한 3개 업체 과점체계에서 모든 업체가 뒤쳐지지 않기 위해 모두 증설을 선택한다. 즉, 공급량 증가 투자가 이뤄지고 시장에 풀리게 되는 순간 공급량은 필연적으로 엄청나게 많아지게 된다.
(현재 기준 3개업체 DRAM Wafer 월 투입량은 총 ~130만장 정도로 보고 있음).

8. 위와 같은 이유로 메모리는 수요폭증>가격상승>공급폭증>가격하

quoted.text:
The math is fine. The accounting is wrong.

When a fund pays out 11%, its price drops by that amount. That's not income. It's a withdrawal with less control over taxes and timing than selling shares yourself.

What matters is total return. If the fund earns 6% and pays 11%, you're eating 5% of your principal every year. The "paycheck" shrinks each year and inflation and taxes make it worse. Those yields usually come from covered calls or return of capital, which cap your upside and leave you with the downside. 

Take the popular "distribution Yield" funds for example. QQQI sells call options on the Nasdaq 100. That premium is the "income," but it means handing someone else your gains above a certain level. You keep the downside and give up part of the upside thinking you got safer "income" when you actually locked in a lower total return. 

And the upside is where stock returns come from, usually in a few sharp rallies after selloffs. In April 2026 alone, QQQ returned about 15.7% to QQQI's 10.3%. Add a 0.68% fee versus 0.18% for QQQ and it falls further behind. It wins in flat markets, but the longer you hold the longer you give up the compound upside trend. 

Here's the actual "paycheck" result using the OP example. Both accounts paid out the exact same paychecks on the exact same days. The one that "sold shares" just has more left because it didn't pay the high fees or cap its upside with covered call "income".

posts.text:
Today marked Day 3 of the latest rally attempts in both the Nasdaq and S&P 500. The earliest a follow-through day could occur is tomorrow. Ideally, one develops between Days 4 and 7, although valid follow-through days can occur later.

No bull market or major uptrend has ever begun without a preceding follow-through day. However, a follow-through day alone does not guarantee a sustained advance. The real test is the quality and breadth of leadership. A healthy uptrend requires several groups of institutional-quality growth stocks, preferably early in their cycles, to lead the way.

Despite the poor technical condition of the major indexes, a surprising number of sound setups are progressing across traditional growth sectors. However, these isolated pockets of strength should not be mistaken for healthy market leadership. With just 145 new highs versus 325 new lows today, most stocks are not participating.

The disconnect is unmistakable: select growth stocks are showing promise, but the broader market continues to deteriorate. Until participation broadens meaningfully, the foundation for a sustainable advance simply isn't there.

I remain 100% in cash. A follow-through day accompanied by broadening, healthy leadership would warrant a change in stance. Until then, I'll let the market earn my participation and keep following my rules. As Bill O’Neil famously said, “The market doesn't care what you think or how you feel, which is why you have to have rules!”

Stay patient, refine your watchlists, update your alerts, and be ready when conditions improve.

posts.name: EndGame Macro
posts.text:
I agree that headline inflation introduces volatility into real wage measurements and that average hourly earnings can be distorted by changes in employment composition. His argument that wage growth was overstated during 2025 is plausible. But where I strongly disagree is the implication that the subsequent deterioration is largely statistical noise. The Employment Cost Index controls for changes in employment composition, yet private sector wage growth still declined from 3.6% in September 2025 to 3.1% in September 2026. More importantly, inflation adjusted wages declined 0.6%.

Using core inflation may produce a smoother trend, but households cannot exclude food, gasoline or heating costs from their budgets. What concerns me most is what neither chart adequately captures, the deterioration in workers’ actual earning capacity. October’s employment report showed declining hours among production and nonsupervisory employees, while involuntary part time employment increased by 339,000. Real weekly earnings for those workers fell 0.3%.

In a low hire, low fire labor market, employers can reduce hours, freeze hiring and limit wage increases long before widespread layoffs emerge. Combine that with restrictive monetary policy and an unresolved energy shock, and the problem becomes considerably more serious. When even the measure designed to eliminate composition distortions shows declining real wages, while workers lose hours and essential costs remain elevated, dismissing the deterioration as statistical noise risks overlooking genuine demand destruction already developing beneath the surface.

quoted.text:
1/ Since real wage growth discourse is back, a reminder: using headline inflation introduces a lot of noise.

posts.name: Meb Faber
posts.text: Very important take, even though inflation is down, it's still at a higher plateau and that's what people care about.

quoted.text:
We have record GDP, record stock prices, record wealth, near record median real wages, etc. So why is sentiment so bad? 

It's mostly what I would call a "price level shock". People view raises as something they earned and price increases as something done to them, so “real incomes are up” doesn’t always register as a positive.

Economists measure inflation as a rate of change (and it's about average now). Consumers feel it as a *cumulative* price shock (and that's near a 30 year high). Gas being at $5 might be a low rate of inflation, but we remember clearly when it was $3. That cumulative effect impacts sentiment.  

Check out these charts. It doesn't explain all of sentiment, but it explains a lot of it. When cumulative inflation is low sentiment is good. When it's up sentiment is bad.

posts.name: Cullen Roche
posts.text:
We have record GDP, record stock prices, record wealth, near record median real wages, etc. So why is sentiment so bad? 

It's mostly what I would call a "price level shock". People view raises as something they earned and price increases as something done to them, so “real incomes are up” doesn’t always register as a positive.

Economists measure inflation as a rate of change (and it's about average now). Consumers feel it as a *cumulative* price shock (and that's near a 30 year high). Gas being at $5 might be a low rate of inflation, but we remember clearly when it was $3. That cumulative effect impacts sentiment.  

Check out these charts. It doesn't explain all of sentiment, but it explains a lot of it. When cumulative inflation is low sentiment is good. When it's up sentiment is bad.

quoted.text:
Very thought-provoking argument by Louis-Vincent Gave @gave_vincent, co-founder and CEO of Gavekal (one of the most respected macro research firms on China).

His argument - which is correct - is that one of the The biggest problem for Western governments today (be it France, the UK, the US) is the rapidly rising cost of funding their debt.

He says that governments have 3 broad ways to get it under control:

1) Austerity, cutting spending massively, which basically no politician wants to do because it makes you massively unpopular

2) Specific to the US, they could dramatically reduce AI data center spending, which soaks up a huge share of the world’s capital and pushes up borrowing costs for everyone, governments included. Not good either since it kills the AI boom.

3) Or, they can go back to embracing China, which he calls "the one deflationary force in the world today." He says it's by far the easiest path, and policymakers always take the easiest path.

Louis-Vincent argues that's exactly what Mark Carney (“the least dumb of the western leaders today,” in Gave’s words) did when he opened Canada to Chinese cars: it's a cheap and easy way to fight inflation, and to reduce the cost of funding Canada’s debt in the process.

It's fairly ironic when you think about it: you can actually find plenty of quotes by Western officials castigating China for "exporting deflation" (like Klaas Knot from the European Central Bank here: https://en.protothema.gr/2024/12/30/ecb-alarm-bell-f

posts.name: Steve Burns
posts.text:
Inflation is driven by four primary mechanisms that reduce purchasing power across the economy: 

1. Monetary expansion. Excessive currency creation by central banks or governments increases the money supply faster than economic output, lowering the value of each dollar. 

2. Demand-pull pressure. Consumer, business, or government spending grows faster than the available supply of goods and services, prompting sellers to raise prices. 

3. Cost-push increases. Rising production expenses: such as higher costs for raw materials, energy, or supply chain inputs, force businesses to pass those added costs on to consumers. 

4. Built-in inflation. Shared expectations of future price increases lead workers to demand higher wages and companies to preemptively raise prices, creating a self-reinforcing cycle.

quoted.text:
China’s record trade surplus raises fresh concerns over global trade imbalances

China’s year-to-date trade surplus reached a record USD 1.04 trillion in October, surpassing USD 958 billion during the same period last year and USD 790 billion in 2024. The widening imbalance highlights the continued strength of China’s export sector, even as domestic demand remains relatively subdued, reinforcing concerns that excess industrial capacity is increasingly being directed towards overseas markets.

During the first ten months of the year, China’s trade surplus with the EU reached a record USD 310 billion, already exceeding the USD 292 billion recorded for the whole of last year. Meanwhile, surpluses with Southeast Asia and the US climbed to USD 293 billion and USD 266.5 billion, respectively, up around 34% and 14% year on year.

October nevertheless brought some narrowing of the monthly surplus to USD 105.3 billion, below expectations, as imports surged partly driven by stronger purchases of crude oil, in dollar terms the strongest since 2022, and refined petroleum products, with both recording their biggest increase since March.

October highlights:
Crude: 9.9 mb/d, +9.4% m/m, -13.3% y/y
Refined Products: 3.15m tonnes, +70% m/m, -10% y/y
Copper:  2.17m tonnes, -13% m/m, -11.6% y/y
Soybeans: 7.35m tonnes, -38% m/m, -22.5% y/y

posts.name: L. Wayne Mathison
posts.text:
I spent much of my life in business, farming and municipal politics. One lesson stands out: good intentions mean very little if the results are poor. You cannot manage a business, operate a farm or run a community indefinitely on promises, excuses and public relations.

Yet somehow, we’ve allowed governments to do exactly that.

Canada has added millions of people, expanded government, increased spending and celebrated economic growth while ordinary Canadians struggle to afford homes, access healthcare and maintain their standard of living.

We have confused activity with achievement, spending with investment, and political virtue with competent government.

I have no objection to immigration when it serves Canada’s interests and our capacity to accommodate newcomers. But bringing people into a country without adequate housing, infrastructure, healthcare or economic opportunities is irresponsible. The consequences fall on Canadians and newcomers alike.

Trudeau perfected the politics of good intentions. Announce an ambitious goal, attach enough moral language to discourage criticism, spend billions and declare success before measuring the outcome.

Now we have Mark Carney, a man who speaks the language of economics, financial markets and technical expertise. That’s an improvement in presentation, but presentation is not performance.

Carney’s greatest political advantage may also be his greatest weakness. He can make political decisions sound like mathematical necessities. But economic models depend on assumptions, and assumptions reflect human judgment. They deserve scrutiny, not automatic obedience.

Experts should inform democracy, not replace it.

I also question the unhealthy financial relationships between government, universities and media organizations. Public funding does not automatically compromise independence, but institutions that depend heavily on government money should face greater scrutiny, not less.

We need universities that teach students how to think, media that challenge authority regardless of political affiliation, and public institutions that measure success by results rather than the size of their budgets.

My political philosophy is straightforward. Government has legitimate responsibilities, but every level must be accountable for fulfilling them. Individual rights, personal responsibility, free enterprise and the rule of law are essential to a prosperous society.

And prosperity must mean something beyond aggregate GDP.

Can young Canadians afford homes? Are real incomes improving? Is productivity increasing? Can families find doctors? Can businesses invest and expand without fighting endless regulatory obstacles?

These are the questions that matter.

A country’s success cannot be measured by how many people it imports, how much money its government spends or how impressive its politicians sound at international conferences.

It must be measured by the opportunities, freedoms and standard of living available to the people who call it home.

I don’t want to return to some imaginary golden age. I want Canada to recover the principles that made prosperity possible: productive work, responsible government, independent thought, accountability and respect for individual achievement.

And I refuse to accept that questioning government policy somehow makes a Canadian intolerant, selfish or disloyal.

Criticism is an essential part of democracy. Politicians work for citizens, not the other way around.

Canada doesn’t need another national narrative telling us how wonderful we are.

It needs competent leadership willing to confront how badly certain policies have failed, explain the trade-offs and deliver measurable improvements.

Because when a government becomes better at explaining failure than correcting it, the problem is no longer communication.

The problem is government itself.

posts.name: Jason Furman
posts.text:
As I said in the note, not my favorite model to use for tariffs.

On your issue, the fall in tariff-related equipment prices in FRB/US is an artifact of consumer prices up, it doesn't want overall prices up by as much, so it forces the residual into investment prices.

Plus the cost to a business is the equipment plus the customs duty, and FRB/US doesn't handle that.

Overall capital goods paid about one-third of tariffs, inputs up in price, and past episodes seem to have reduced investment.

That said, tariffs affect different industries very differently and in some your effect would predominate. Unfortunately FRB/US doesn't have industries so can't model that--why it's not my favorite model for this.

posts.name: Puru Saxena
posts.text:
The Democratic midterm sweep has raised valid questions about the AI data centre buildout. The reality is more nuanced than the recent market reaction suggests.

2027 capacity looks largely intact. Most projects scheduled to come online next year are already under construction and newly elected governors are not expected to disrupt work that has started. Hyperscaler capex forecasts for 2027 remain essentially unchanged.

The risk sits further out. Roughly 20% of planned US capacity for 2028 (about 5 GW) could slip into 2029, mainly in Texas and Ohio, as new permitting and utility rules are written. This creates a potential air pocket for parts of the supply chain in 2028, but it is a delay not a cancellation.

Power constraints and interconnection queues were already going to push some projects later. Politics is now an additional variable, not the sole driver.

The AI infrastructure cycle is being extended, it is not ending. For quality names with strong free cash flow, durable backlogs and pricing power, the recent selloff looks more like a sentiment reset than a fundamental one. It pays to be greedy when others are fearful.
